question: Can a vision-style masked autoencoder learn reusable embeddings of full two-dimensional LLM attention maps at corpus scale, and can clusters of those embeddings predict next-token correctness and identify attention heads whose suppression improves Java code completion?

key_findings.claim: AP-MAE reconstructs held-out masked attention maps from the StarCoder2 model size on which it was trained and retains the same loss scale when evaluated across the 3B, 7B, and 15B family, although the worst cross-size increase is substantial in relative terms.
key_findings.evidence: The nine train/evaluate losses, in units of 10^-3 with the paper's parenthesized dispersion, are 3B-trained: 7.07 (2.12), 7.78 (2.05), 9.53 (2.76); 7B-trained: 7.55 (2.05), 7.17 (2.12), 9.29 (2.66); and 15B-trained: 9.57 (3.35), 10.05 (3.79), 7.59 (2.42). Thus every cross-size mean remains below 0.0101, but 15B-trained evaluation on 7B is about 40% above the matched 7B loss. The paper supplies no trivial, convolutional, or non-MAE reconstruction baseline with which to interpret absolute fidelity.

key_findings.claim: Logarithmic preprocessing is necessary for the reported AP-MAE training recipe, but the ablation establishes that conclusion only visually.
key_findings.evidence: The raw-attention model produces visibly corrupted masked patches, while the log-scaled model reconstructs the major patterns. The authors explicitly say the loss values cannot be compared, report no repeated-run statistic, and do not test other monotone transforms; consequently Figure 1 supports recipe dependence, not a quantitative advantage of the natural logarithm over alternatives.

key_findings.claim: Per-head clustering recovers visually recurring attention motifs, including diagonals, vertical stripes, and repeated square-like structures, but the paper does not quantitatively validate a discovered taxonomy.
key_findings.evidence: For each of up to 1,920 heads, 512-dimensional AP-MAE embeddings from about 110,000 task samples are reduced to eight UMAP dimensions and clustered with HDBSCAN. Figures 2 and 3 show hand-selected examples and cluster counts; the identification of induction-like, rare-token-like, and allegedly undocumented square motifs is qualitative, with no cluster-stability, retrieval, annotation-agreement, or cross-model cluster-alignment metric. The authors also note that related square motifs at different scales land in different clusters.

key_findings.claim: Categorical cluster assignments contain a modest, task-dependent signal about whether a next-token prediction is correct.
key_findings.evidence: A separate CatBoost classifier per task receives one categorical cluster ID per head, using 10,000 task inputs balanced between correct and incorrect generations. Reported ten-fold cross-validation accuracy is about 55–60% for identifiers, Boolean literals, and string literals, comparable to the random-mask task; End-of-Line reaches just over 70% for StarCoder2-15B. Chance is 50%, confidence intervals across folds are narrow, and classification accuracy is reported as uncorrelated with the target model's own next-token accuracy.

key_findings.claim: The classifier's SHAP signal is sparse and task-specific, but it is associative evidence rather than a causal decomposition of attention-head function.
key_findings.evidence: For End-of-Line and the other nine classified tasks, only a small subset of heads has a large maximum difference in mean SHAP value across cluster categories, and different tasks highlight different heads. The appendix supplies all task/model SHAP maps. Because CatBoost SHAP attributes a predictive model with correlated categorical inputs, it does not by itself show that a head or a particular attention motif causes correctness.

key_findings.claim: Suppressing a selected small set of extreme-SHAP heads can improve accuracy on the paper's balanced intervention panels, while suppressing larger sets produces abrupt total failure.
key_findings.evidence: Each condition contains 1,000 originally correct and 1,000 originally incorrect cases. The largest reported End-of-Line gain is 271 net correct cases for StarCoder2-15B, equivalent to 13.55 percentage points on that balanced 2,000-case panel; the largest String-Literal gain is 112 cases for 3B, or 5.6 points. Collapse makes all 1,000 originally correct cases wrong and corrects none of the originally wrong cases. For 3B, collapse occurs around 200 positive/100 negative ranked heads on String Literal and 400/200 on End-of-Line; for 7B it is about 200/200 and 400/400, respectively.

key_findings.claim: The 13.6% intervention headline is a selected maximum, not a demonstrated out-of-sample improvement on the natural task distribution.
key_findings.evidence: The paper searches head-counts from 1 to 800, three SHAP groups, ten tasks, and three model sizes, then highlights the largest balanced-panel net gain. It does not describe a separate intervention-selection versus evaluation split, uncertainty for the task-level maxima, or multiplicity correction. It also zeroes the same task-ranked heads across a condition rather than selecting a pattern-conditioned edit for each inference. These omissions prevent interpreting 13.6% as a deployment-level causal effect of AP-MAE classification.

key_findings.claim: The evaluation protocol is not fully reproducible from the manuscript because its stated classifier split is arithmetically inconsistent and clustering appears transductive.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6.2 says ten-fold cross-validation uses a '90, 10, 10 split,' which totals 110%, without defining train/validation/test roles. Section 5.1 clusters all task embeddings per head before the classifier split is introduced, so held-out classifier examples apparently influence unsupervised UMAP/HDBSCAN geometry. This does not prove label leakage, but it means the reported folds are not a fully inductive end-to-end test.

key_findings.claim: The proposed 'resource race between competing circuits' is an author hypothesis, not an experimentally isolated mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: The observed gain-then-collapse curve is compatible with several explanations, including redundancy, correlated ranking, distribution shift after ablation, or ordinary loss of capacity. The authors explicitly introduce the resource-race account with 'we believe' and state that it requires more research; there is no circuit reconstruction or competing-path intervention.

method.core_idea: Treat each causal attention matrix as a one-channel image, learn a fixed-size representation with a masked vision transformer, and mine those representations instead of manually defining attention-pattern heuristics.
method.mechanism: The pipeline truncates StarCoder2 Java contexts to 256 tokens, log-scales attention weights, masks half of 32-by-32 image patches, and trains separate 24-layer-encoder/eight-layer-decoder AP-MAEs on 72 million attention patterns sampled only from correct random-mask generations. For eleven mined completion tasks, the 512-dimensional CLS embedding of every head is reduced and clustered separately with UMAP and HDBSCAN. A per-task CatBoost model uses the resulting head-wise cluster IDs to classify correctness; mean SHAP differences rank heads, whose output contributions are then zeroed in increasing sets during intervention.
assumptions: The two-dimensional geometry of a 256-token attention matrix contains stable functional information that survives logarithmic scaling and patch masking.
Training only on attention patterns from correct random-mask predictions still yields useful embeddings for incorrect generations and ten structurally different Java tasks.
Fixed-length Java completions from one decontaminated dataset and one model family are informative proxies for broader LLM behavior.
Per-head UMAP/HDBSCAN clusters are stable enough that their arbitrary categorical IDs can support reproducible prediction and head ranking.
CatBoost SHAP association is sufficiently aligned with causal head contribution to choose useful ablations.
Zeroing a head's contribution is a meaningful local intervention rather than an out-of-distribution perturbation that induces unrelated compensation or collapse.
Balanced correct/incorrect panels and fold-level confidence intervals approximate the quantities needed in naturally imbalanced deployment settings.

techniques.role: Learns a 512-dimensional representation by reconstructing masked patches of a causal attention matrix treated as an image.
Compresses dominant attention weights so reconstruction is not governed only by a few high-intensity tokens.
Uses Java parsing to extract repeated identifier, literal, operator, statement-ending, random-mask, and noise scenarios from uncurated code.
Runs UMAP to eight dimensions and HDBSCAN separately for each attention head to assign recurring pattern categories at tens to hundreds of millions of pattern observations.
Feeds one attention-pattern cluster ID per head into a task-specific CatBoost classifier for correct-versus-incorrect next-token prediction.
Ranks heads by differences in mean classifier SHAP values and sets selected attention-head contributions to zero to test task accuracy effects.
Uses The Heap, which was deduplicated against StarCoder2 training data, to reduce code-completion contamination.

evaluations.setting: Three AP-MAEs trained separately on 72M correct-generation attention patterns from StarCoder2-3B, 7B, or 15B; 256-token maps; 50% mask ratio; 150,000 batches; eight A100 GPUs; under 100 GPU-hours
evaluations.metric: Masked reconstruction loss, reported as mean (dispersion) ×10^-3
evaluations.result: Matched losses are 7.07 (2.12), 7.17 (2.12), and 7.59 (2.42) for 3B, 7B, and 15B; all cross-size losses range from 7.55 to 10.05
evaluations.baseline: Only matched-size AP-MAE is used as a baseline; no trivial predictor, alternative encoder, or cheaper vision model is evaluated

evaluations.setting: Log-scaled versus raw attention-map preprocessing with otherwise identical AP-MAE architecture
evaluations.result: Major motifs are visibly reconstructed after log scaling, while raw-scale masked patches appear corrupted
evaluations.baseline: The authors state numerical losses are not comparable, so the ablation has no quantitative baseline or uncertainty

evaluations.setting: Eleven Java task streams; 10,000 inputs per task, balanced correct/incorrect; 720 to 1,920 categorical head features; ten-fold CatBoost cross-validation
evaluations.result: Approximately 55–60% on several tasks and just over 70% for StarCoder2-15B End-of-Line
evaluations.baseline: 50% balanced chance; random masking is about 55–60%; hidden-state, raw-attention, confidence, entropy, and calibrated uncertainty baselines are absent

evaluations.setting: Per-task/model SHAP analysis over CatBoost cluster features
evaluations.metric: Maximum difference in mean SHAP value across a head's cluster categories
evaluations.result: Maps are sparse and select different heads across tasks; sparsity appears greater in larger models
evaluations.baseline: No stability across seeds, alternative attribution method, or quantitative sparsity statistic is reported

evaluations.setting: Per-condition head-zeroing on 1,000 originally correct plus 1,000 originally incorrect generations; ranked positive, negative, neutral, and random heads; 1–800 heads
evaluations.metric: Net correct cases: incorrect-to-correct conversions minus correct-to-incorrect conversions
evaluations.result: Maximum +271 cases for StarCoder2-15B End-of-Line (13.55 points on the balanced panel) and +112 for StarCoder2-3B String Literal (5.6 points), followed by abrupt collapse for extreme-SHAP rankings
evaluations.baseline: Random and near-neutral head removal decline more gradually; the paper does not report a separately held-out head-count selection set or task-level confidence interval

evaluations.setting: Qualitative pattern mining across 79.2M, 126.7M, and 211.2M head-pattern observations for StarCoder2-3B, 7B, and 15B
evaluations.metric: Visual motif recurrence and clusters per head
evaluations.result: Diagonal, stripe, combined, and multi-scale square motifs are displayed; some noise inputs lack the square structures
evaluations.baseline: No annotated motif benchmark, retrieval precision, cluster stability, or cross-model taxonomy metric is supplied

limitations: Author-stated: every attention map is forced to a 256-token input length, so sequence-length variation and long-context behavior are untested.
Author-stated: the 126M-parameter vision-transformer autoencoder is computationally expensive, and Bags of Visual Words, VLAD, CNNs, or other cheaper detectors are not included as baselines.
Author-stated: the eleven parser-selected tasks cover only a subset of possible behavior, task-to-task variance is large, and mechanistic-interpretability tasks lack a general formalization.
Author-stated: evaluation is restricted to Java; extension to natural language would rely on ambiguous, probabilistic parsing whose errors may change the results.
Author-stated: AP-MAE identifies patterns and regions of interest but does not explain the detailed computation of a circuit.
Author-stated: the MAE's whole-image objective separates related motifs appearing at different spatial scales, motivating more compositional detectors.
Author-stated: AP-MAE training excludes incorrect generations because anomalous attention outliers might prevent convergence, leaving that selection's effect unknown.

Reviewer-identified: all target models are StarCoder2 checkpoints and all substantive tasks are one-token Java completions; reconstruction transfer across sizes is not transfer across architectures, domains, context lengths, or generation regimes.

Reviewer-identified: absolute reconstruction loss has no simple, convolutional, raw-pixel, or alternative-transform baseline, and the claimed pattern taxonomy is supported by selected visual examples rather than quantitative validation.
Reviewer-identified: the written '90, 10, 10' classifier split is impossible as stated, and clustering the complete dataset before cross-validation makes the pipeline transductive.

Reviewer-identified: balanced accuracy alone omits AUROC, precision-recall, calibration, prevalence sensitivity, and comparisons to ordinary output confidence, entropy, hidden states, or raw attention statistics.

Reviewer-identified: the maximum intervention gain is selected over many tasks, model sizes, ranking signs, and head counts without a distinct selection/evaluation split, repeated-run uncertainty, or multiplicity control.

Reviewer-identified: interventions suppress globally ranked heads for every example rather than editing a particular detected pattern online, so they do not establish that a discovered cluster is the causal unit.
Reviewer-identified: end-to-end cost for 720–1,920 independent UMAP/HDBSCAN jobs plus classifier training is not reported against automated-circuit or lightweight-attention baselines.
failure_modes: Attention motifs may shift with context length, padding, tokenization, architecture, rotary-position scaling, grouped-query attention, or a non-code domain, invalidating a fixed 256-by-256 encoder.
An AP-MAE trained only on correct generations may map erroneous or anomalous attention patterns arbitrarily, making apparent correctness clusters artifacts of out-of-distribution encoding.
UMAP and HDBSCAN instability can change categorical cluster IDs and downstream SHAP rankings even if the underlying attention maps change little.
Correctness classifiers can exploit confidence, token frequency, prompt position, or task difficulty correlates rather than a mechanism responsible for the predicted token.
Correlated heads make CatBoost SHAP credit non-identifiable; suppressing one ranked head can expose compensation that the observational classifier never modeled.
A head-zeroing edit is far outside the model's training distribution and can cause wholesale collapse before revealing the normal function of the head.
Multi-scale or translated versions of the same local motif may be assigned to separate clusters because the MAE represents the whole image.
A task-level intervention chosen at its best head count can regress on a natural, imbalanced, or shifted stream even when it improves the balanced analysis panel.
reusable_insights: Two-dimensional internal signals can be embedded with vision objectives before applying more expensive mechanistic tools, but the embedding needs task-relevant and stability baselines.
A monotone intensity transform can prevent sparse high-magnitude attention entries from dominating reconstruction objectives.
Structured domains such as code permit corpus-scale repetition mining without hand-writing every prompt template.
Correctness may be distributed across many weak head-level signals even when only a few heads dominate a fitted classifier's attribution map.
Intervention sweeps should report both the small-edit benefit regime and the catastrophic capacity-loss regime rather than only the best point.
Association-based component ranking becomes much more useful when followed by held-out causal interventions, explicit random/neutral controls, and a preregistered selection rule.
Pattern discovery and mechanistic explanation are distinct stages: a scalable screen can prioritize components without itself identifying a circuit.
open_questions: Do AP-MAE embeddings and cluster neighborhoods transfer across different model families, attention variants, languages, and variable context lengths?
How stable are per-head UMAP/HDBSCAN assignments and SHAP rankings across random seeds, data subsets, and clustering hyperparameters?
Can a jointly learned, cross-head embedding produce an aligned motif taxonomy instead of thousands of unrelated per-head label spaces?
Does AP-MAE add predictive value over output probability, entropy, hidden-state probes, and simple attention statistics on a fully inductive held-out pipeline?
Can a pattern-conditioned, per-example edit outperform global task-level head zeroing while avoiding collapse?
Which discovered square motifs correspond to a reproducible causal computation under path patching, activation patching, or circuit reconstruction?
Does training AP-MAE on incorrect as well as correct generations improve anomaly detection or instead destabilize reconstruction?
What is the compute/quality Pareto frontier among MAEs, CNNs, hand-crafted motif features, and direct attention-map classifiers?

competitive_landscape.title: Motifs in Attention Patterns of Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Ivanitskiy et al. compute explicit features of attention matrices, use PCA to embed patterns, derive distances between heads, and build an Attentionpedia-style similarity tool across models. AP-MAE instead learns the pattern embedding through masked image reconstruction, clusters every head separately at much larger code-task scale, and adds correctness classification and ablation; it does not provide the concurrent work's aligned head-distance interface or quantitative comparison.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2025 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop poster; OpenReview last modified 2025-12-06

competitive_landscape.title: Lookback Lens: Detecting and Mitigating Contextual Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Only Attention Maps
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct prior attention-based correctness detector and mitigation method
competitive_landscape.difference: Lookback Lens uses a transparent per-head ratio of attention to context versus generated tokens, obtains cross-task and 7B-to-13B transfer, and guides candidate decoding to improve XSum correctness by 9.6 points. AP-MAE uses learned full-matrix cluster categories for single-token Java correctness, demonstrates only reconstruction transfer among StarCoder2 sizes, and mitigates errors by globally zeroing ranked heads rather than choosing decoded candidates.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv v2; EMNLP 2024 main-conference long paper

competitive_landscape.title: Gradient-guided Attention Map Editing: Towards Efficient Contextual Hallucination Mitigation
competitive_landscape.difference: GAME trains a classifier to flag hallucination-prone attention maps and uses gradient-derived edit directions to redistribute attention at inference across multiple models and summarization/QA tasks, reporting a 10% XSum reduction. AP-MAE learns an unsupervised image embedding and discovers motifs at greater corpus scale, but its intervention removes whole task-ranked heads and does not condition an edit on the current map.

competitive_landscape.title: Shapley Head Pruning: Identifying and Removing Interference in Multilingual Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct prior head-attribution and beneficial-pruning method
competitive_landscape.difference: Held and Yang approximate coalition-based Shapley values for attention heads and prune negative-value language-specific heads to reduce multilingual interference on sentence classification and structural prediction. AP-MAE attributes cluster-category features with CatBoost SHAP, targets Java next-token correctness, and adds learned two-dimensional motif discovery, but its SHAP values are predictive-model attributions rather than head coalition values.
competitive_landscape.source_version: EACL 2023 official ACL Anthology proceedings record

competitive_landscape.title: On the weak link between importance and prunability of attention heads
competitive_landscape.relationship: direct negative-result prior for the attribution-to-pruning inference
competitive_landscape.difference: Prasanna et al. find that many Transformer/BERT heads can be randomly pruned and that previously interpreted importance or layer location does not reliably improve pruning decisions. AP-MAE reports a stronger separation between extreme-SHAP and random/neutral removal on selected code tasks, but does not benchmark against causal or gradient head-importance methods and selects the best intervention point over many sweeps.
competitive_landscape.source_version: EMNLP 2020 official ACL Anthology proceedings record

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
competitive_landscape.difference: ACDC automates edge-level circuit discovery against a task metric and validates recovered component types on known small-model circuits. AP-MAE is a cheaper, behavior-scale screen over attention-pattern shape and can rank heads across millions of natural code observations, but it neither recovers connections nor verifies that selected heads constitute a circuit.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first scalable vision-model treatment of full LLM attention patterns that reconstructs and mines recurring structures, transfers across model sizes, predicts correctness without ground truth, and guides accuracy-improving head interventions on noisy real-world code.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper does contribute an unusually large learned pipeline: 72M-pattern AP-MAE training, 79.2M–211.2M per-model task-pattern analysis, syntax-mined decontaminated Java inputs, a full two-dimensional embedding rather than one handcrafted attention statistic, and an end-to-end bridge from clustering to prediction and ablation. Primary records show, however, that full attention-motif embeddings, attention-only correctness classifiers, cross-model detectors, classifier-guided attention edits, SHAP/Shapley-based beneficial head pruning, and automated circuit localization all predate or are concurrent with AP-MAE.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the particular scale and integration of a masked vision autoencoder with syntax-mined code scenarios and per-head motif clustering—not the general ideas that attention maps predict errors or that attributed heads can be intervened on. The classification and 13.6-point balanced-panel maximum are promising screens, but the inconsistent split, transductive clustering, absent ordinary uncertainty baselines, qualitative motif validation, and unseparated intervention selection prevent strong claims of generalizable correctness detection or discovered causal circuits.

reviewer_notes: Secondary verification covered all 27 extracted pages, including the full references, all SHAP maps (Figures 8–17), and every task-level intervention plot (Figures 18–27); source hashes were independently recomputed and match the fulltext index. Quantitative statements distinguish table/text values from visual ranges: Figure 4 does not print exact bar labels, so classifier results are retained at the precision used by the authors. The reported 13.6% is normalized to the explicitly balanced 2,000-case panel and is not treated as a natural-prevalence gain. Author limitations and the speculative resource-race explanation are labeled separately from reviewer audits. Six competitor records were checked at primary arXiv, OpenReview, ACL Anthology, or NeurIPS proceedings pages current through 2026-08-23. Remaining uncertainty is protocol-level: the manuscript does not resolve what '90, 10, 10' means, whether intervention cases are disjoint from classifier/clustering data, or how the best head count was selected.

verification.passage_check: Checked every finding against the page-marked local v1/TMLR text and inspected the local PDF for Tables 1–2, Figure 4 bar ranges, Figure 7 intervention framing, all stated limitations, and appendices A–B. Recomputed both PDF and extracted-text SHA-256 pins and confirmed 27/27 pages have usable text.
verification.competitor_check: Inspected the primary abstracts/full records and, where needed, rendered paper text for Motifs in Attention Patterns, Lookback Lens, GAME, Shapley Head Pruning, the weak-link pruning negative result, and ACDC. Verified canonical IDs, exact titles, venues/versions, direct methodological overlap, and that the target paper itself is excluded.
